Dublin on foot

Wizzy knows 50 places in Dublin, from the big sights to the corners most people walk straight past. Start a walk, put your phone away, and Wizzy taps you on the shoulder when there's something worth looking up at.

The must-sees

  • Book of Kells and the Old Library

    Museum

    The Book of Kells was made by monks around the year 800 and is one of the great treasures of early medieval art. The Long Room, finished in the 1730s, holds about 200,000 of the library’s oldest books.

  • Christ Church Cathedral

    Church

    It was founded around 1030 under the Norse king Sitric Silkbeard. Its large medieval crypt holds curiosities including a mummified cat and rat.

    Look for: In the nave lies a knight’s tomb said to be Strongbow’s. The original was smashed when the roof fell in 1562, and a similar effigy replaced it.

  • Dublin Castle

    Palace

    King John ordered a castle built here in 1204, and for seven centuries it was the seat of British rule in Ireland. In January 1922 it was handed over to Michael Collins and the new Irish government.

    Look for: Above the gate, the statue of Justice faces into the castle with her back to the city, a detail Dubliners long took as a pointed joke.

  • General Post Office

    Landmark · 1818

    Francis Johnston’s building was the headquarters of the rebels in the 1916 Easter Rising, and Patrick Pearse read the Proclamation of the Irish Republic outside. A museum inside tells the story.

    Look for: Look closely at the front columns: they are still pitted with bullet marks from 1916.

  • Guinness Storehouse

    Museum

    Arthur Guinness signed a 9,000-year lease on the brewery site in 1759. The storehouse tells the brewery’s story and ends in the rooftop Gravity Bar, with views across the city.

    Look for: The glass atrium at the heart of the building is shaped like a giant pint glass.

  • Ha’penny Bridge

    Bridge · 1816

    Opened in 1816, it took its nickname from the halfpenny toll charged to cross. It was the only pedestrian bridge over the Liffey for many years.

  • Kilmainham Gaol

    Museum · 1796

    Many Irish rebels were held here, and in May 1916 fourteen leaders of the Easter Rising were executed in its Stonebreakers’ Yard. It closed in 1924 and was restored by volunteers from the 1960s.

  • Phoenix Park

    Park · 1662

    It was created in 1662 as a royal deer park. It also holds the President’s residence, Dublin Zoo and the Papal Cross, where Pope John Paul II said Mass in 1979.

    Look for: Find the Wellington Monument, a granite obelisk over 60 metres high, the tallest in Europe.

  • St Stephen’s Green

    Park

    It was a private park for residents until 1880, when Lord Ardilaun of the Guinness family paid to open it to the public. In 1916 rebels of the Irish Citizen Army dug trenches here.

    Look for: At the Grafton Street corner, the Fusiliers’ Arch honours Irish soldiers killed in the Boer War. Critics nicknamed it Traitors’ Gate.

  • St. Patrick’s Cathedral

    Church · 1191

    It was founded in 1191 near a well where Saint Patrick is said to have baptised converts. Jonathan Swift, author of Gulliver’s Travels, was its dean for over thirty years and is buried inside.

    Look for: Find the door with a hole cut in it. In 1492, the story goes, the Earl of Kildare reached through to shake hands with his rival Ormond: ‘chancing his arm’.

  • Trinity College

    Culture · 1592

    Queen Elizabeth I founded the university in 1592. Jonathan Swift, Oscar Wilde and Samuel Beckett all studied here.

    Look for: Look at the Campanile in Front Square. Students say anyone who walks under it while its bell rings will fail their exams.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Dublin and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Dublin passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
